 Criminal Appeal no. 42/17
 Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector
 In The Court Of Sh. Devender Kumar Jangala
 Asj-05, Patiala House Court, New Delhi District,
 New Delhi
 Dlnd010023002017
 Criminal Appeal no. 42/17
 Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector
26.04.2024
Ajay Kumar
S/o Sh. Nathuni,
Masala Stall, Pilli Kothi Chowk
Bijli Road, Naya Bazar,
Delhi-110006 ......... Appellant
 Versus
Food Inspector
Directorate of Pfa
Government of Nct of Delhi
A-20, Lawrence Road Industrial Area
Delhi-110035 .....Respondent
Date of institution : 19.04.2017
Date of arguments : 16.04.2024
Date of order : 26.04.2024 
Appearances: Sh. G. P. Saxena, Sh. R. P. Pandey and Ms. Ishani,
 Advocates on behalf of appellant. 
 Sh.Vinod Kumar Sharma, Ld. Chief Public
 Prosecutor for respondent/Department. 
 J U D G M E N T:
1. This is an appeal under Section 374(3)(A) Cr.PC challenging the judgment of conviction dated 30.01.2017 and order on Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector the point of sentence dated 03.02.2017 passed by the court of Sh. Ashu Garg, Ld. Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, New Delhi. The Ld. Trial Court vide impugned judgment dated 30.01.2017 had found the appellant guilty of commission of offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a) read with Section 7 of Prevention of Food Adulteration(hereinafter referred as PFA) Act and vide order dated 03.02.2017 sentenced him to undergo one year simple imprisonment and to pay fine of Rs.25,000/- for the offence punishable Ajay Kumar vs Food Inspector on 26 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/40683698/
1 under Section 16(1)(a) read with Section 7 of PFA Act and to undergo simple imprisonment for 15 days in dafault of payment of fine. 
2. Arguments on the appeal on behalf of appellant were advanced by Mr.G. P. Saxena, Advocate and Sh. Vinod Kumar Sharma, Ld. Chief Public Prosecutor has represented the respondent department. 
Record perused. 
3. Brief facts: It is alleged that on 19.04.2011, Food Inspector S. B. Singh purchased a sample of Kali Mirch from the appellant Ajay Kumar under the supervision of Local Health Authority(LHA)/SDM for analysis. The said sample was sent to the Public Analysist who declared the alleged sample adulterated because it found containing 'mineral oil' and did not confirm to the standard because 'light berries' exceeds beyond the prescribed limit. On the basis of report of Public Analysist complaint dated 28.06.2011 was filed by Food Inspector. The appellant in exercise of his right under Section 13(2) of PFA get the sample analyzed by the central laboratory who also declared the sample adulterated because of presence of 'mineral oil' etc in the sampled article. 
Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector 4. The Ld. Trial Court after framing of notice proceeded for trial and recorded the statement of prosecution witnesses. After conclusion of trial, the appellant/accused was convicted vide judgment dated 30.01.2017 and sentenced vide detailed order dated 03.02.2017.
5. The appellant/convict being aggrieved by the order of conviction and order on the point of sentence has filed the present appeal. It is argued that the judgment of Ld.Trial Court is based on prediction and assumptions and suffers from errors of law and appreciation of evidence. That the Ld. Trial Court has passed the judgment against the facts and evidence available on the judicial record. That the Ld. Trial Court has failed to appreciate that the witnesses deposed before the court were against the facts and contradictory to each other. That the sanctioning authority has given the sanction to file the present case against the appellant without application of his mind and without going through the facts of the case. That the reports of both the laboratories were divergent and vague. That the process of lifting the alleged sample by the Food Inspector was not proper and sample was taken without proper mixing, therefore, the report of both the laboratories were wrong and divergent. That the Food Inspector has not tried to associate the independent witness intentionally at the time of sampling. That the documents alleged to be prepared at the spot were not prepared at the spot but prepared later on in the office and the thumb impression of the accused were taken on blank papers. That both the laboratories have not discussed the kind of mineral oil found in the sampled article. It is prayed that in view of grounds of appeal, the Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector impugned judgment dated 30.01.2017 and order on the point of sentence dated 03.02.2017 may kindly be set aside. 
6. Notice of the present appeal was issued to the respondent/department. The respondent/department put appearance being represented by Ld. Chief Public Prosecutor and strongly opposed the appeal filed by the appellant. It is submitted that none of the grounds of appeal are sustainable in the eyes of law. That all the contentions have already been dealt with by the Ld. 
Ajay Kumar vs Food Inspector on 26 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/40683698/
2 Trial Court and there is no illegality or infirmity in the impugned order passed by Ld. Trial Court. It is prayed that the appeal may kindly be dismissed. 
7. I have considered the submissions made on behalf of appellant/convict and Ld. Chief Public Prosecutor for Department and perused the record. 
8. In the present appeal it is contended that that the Ld. Trial Court has fails to appreciate that the witnesses deposed before the court were against the facts and contradictory to each other. However,
the appellant has nowhere described as to how and in which manner the deposition of witnesses were against the facts or contrary to each other. No contradiction emerged in the deposition of witnesses which is fatal to the case of prosecution, is pointed out by the appellant. 
9. It is also argued that the sanctioning authority has given the sanction without application of mind. 
In the present matter the sanction was taken by Food Inspector PW-1 Sh. A. K. Singh from the then Director, PFA and thereafter a complaint Ex. PW1/A was filed in the Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector court. The appellant has fails to disclose any material on record which reflects that the sanction to prosecute was given by Director, PFA without application of mind. In the absence of any material to support this contention, the same is not tenable. 
10. It is also contended that the Ld. Trial Court has fails to appreciate that the reports of both the laboratories were divergent, vague and fictitious. This issue was also raised by the accused before the Ld. Trial Court which dealt with the same in para 15 and 16 of the impugned judgment. The Ld.
Trial Court has dealt with this issue in length and considered various judgments and observed as under:
"A careful study of the said precedents would therefore show that mere differences or variations in report of PA and CFL would not, by themselves, lead to a direct conclusion that the samples were not representative. When a sample is analysed by two different persons, the possibility of variations cannot be ruled out. And precisely for this reason. the report of CFL has been given preference over the report of PA,
considering the Director, CFL to be the better expert. Not only this, the report of CFL is given finality and is declared to be conclusive evidence, after superseding the earlier report of PA. The sample would become all the more prone to variations as there would always be some time gap between the analyses carried out by PA and CFL. But mere delay in analyses by CFL and consequent variations would not be a reason to discard its report, which is otherwise final and conclusive, unless the accused is able to show that the variations are on account of delay in analysing the sample or that some chemical changes during the Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector intervening period had resulted in such variations. Again, this is not a matter or assumptions or presumptions. There is no rule prescribed anywhere that after a particular delay, a sample would be rendered unfit for analysis. The court cannot assume such facts on hypothetical basis and observe that delay would in any case would have frustrated the right of the accused so as to cause prejudice to him. But if the accused is able to lead sufficient evidence or is able to otherwise establish that Ajay Kumar vs Food Inspector on 26 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/40683698/
3 prejudice was in fact cause to him on account of any such delay, benefit would certainly go to him. One such situation in favour of the accused would be when the sample is sent to CFL but it is found to be "unfit for analysis" in which case it can be assumed that the right of the accused stood frustrated. But where despite the delay,
the sample did not get decomposed and remained fit for analysis, or where the accused did not opt to get the sample analysed from CFL, in such cases, there would be no assumption that the sample would have become unfit for analysis or caused prejudice to the accused. It would always be a matter or evidence adduced by the prosecution and defence and not a matter or assumptions".
11. The learned Trial Court has rightly come to observation that there is no rule prescribed under the statute to conclude what variation would be substantial enough to be considered in favour of the accused. The Act or Rules do not prescribe that any variation of more than a specific value or percentage would be a substantial variation so as to disregard the report of the CFL which has otherwise been given finality or conclusiveness. In the absence of any such standard Ajay Kumar Vs.
Food Inspector prescribed, the matter would be governed only by the evidence adduced by the parties, which includes cross-examination of witnesses(subject to cross-examination of course). I am in agreement with the observation made by Ld. Trial Court that no benefit can be granted to the accused merely because there are variations in two reports. If the accused is able to show through evidence that the variations are substantial enough so as to conclude that the sample was not representative, he would get benefit. It is true that in the present case the accused has fails to show that such variations were due to sample being not representative. There is no requirement under the Act or Rules that the two reports should be uniform or identical or that any variation of +- 0.3% in any ingredient would nullify the report of CFL. The view expressed by Ld. Trial Court on this issue are in consonance with the settled principles of law and no interference in this regard is required. 
The CFL report has confirmed the PA report on both the counts, though the percentage of light berries exceeded a little by the time the sample reached the CFL but as far as mineral oil is concerned, the CFL has confirmed the PA report. 
12. It is submitted by Ld.counsel for the appellant/convict that in the present matter the PA report or the CFL report has fails to distinguish whether the mineral oil found in the sample was food grade or not. Ld.counsel for the accused has relied upon one judgment of Hon'ble Delhi High Court reported as 2007(2) JCC 1154 State Vs. Dwarka Dass wherein Hon'ble High Court was pleased to held:
"The report of Public Analyst standards superseded by the report of Director, CFL. 
Prosecution can not fall upon the report of Public Analyst to fill up lacunae or ambiguity in the report of CFL. Since on the basis of report of CFL, which is Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector silent about the mineral oil being food grade or non food grade, the accused has been given benefit of doubt, it would not be appropriate for this court to take other view" 
13. On this issue it is submitted by Ld. Chief Public Prosecutor that existence of mineral oil in the lifted sample is sufficient to constitute the ingredient of commission of offence under PFA and it is Ajay Kumar vs Food Inspector on 26 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/40683698/
4 immaterial where the mineral oil was of food grade or not.
14. The said issue was also raised before the Ld. Trial Court and the Ld. Trial Court has dealt with this issue in detail and observed that neither food grade nor non food grade mineral oil would be permitted for use in case of Kali Mirch in view of Item no. A.05.17 of Appendix B. It is not the defence of the accused that no mineral oil was detected or was detected wrongly. During the course of trial no stand has been taken by the accused that any such oil was as a result of natural involvement or the food article having been exposed to the natural environment. The accused sought to challenge the validity of reports on technical ground, which is not tenable in view of aforesaid observation. There is nothing on record to disbelieve the reports relied upon by the prosecution wherein the mineral oil has been detected in the food article. I am in agreement with the observation made by Ld. Trial Court that existence of mineral oil either food grade or non food grade is sufficient enough to prove the ingredients of alleged offence. 
15. The Ld. Trial Court vide detailed judgment has given clear findings with regard to all the defences taken by the applicant/accused. There is no illegality or infirmity in the impugned judgment of Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector conviction dated 30.01.2017 passed by Ld. Trial Court convicting the appellant for the offences punishable under Section 16(1)(a) of PFA Act. Accordingly,
the appeal against the judgment dated 30.01.2017 passed by the court of Sh. Ashu Garg, Ld.
ACMM-II, New Delhi, Patiala House Courts in CC no. 142/11 is liable to be dismissed. Hence,
dismissed. 
16. The appellant in the present appeal has also challanged the order on the point of sentence. It is argued that the PFA act has been recently amended which prescribed the punishment of fine also. It is prayed that in view of pendency of case for a long period, a lenient view may kindly be taken. On the other hand it is argued on behalf of department by Ld. Chief Public Prosecutor that the Ld. Trial Court has already taken a lenient view and there is no illegality in the order of sentence. 
17. The appellant/convict is convicted for commission of offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)
of PFA Act wherein the minimum sentence of imprisonment was awarded. However, w.e.f.
15.10.2007, new Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 came into force in which, for similar offence,
the punishment of only of fine has been prescribed. 
18. In view of above, question for consideration before this court is whether after repeal of earlier Act and introduction of new Act which contains the lesser punishment, the court can take a lenient view of awarding the lesser punishment. On this issue, I have relied upon one latest judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as M/s A. K. Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector Sarkar &
Company & Anr. Vs. The State of West Bengal & Ors, Special Leave Petition(Criminal) No.6095 of 2018, dated 07.03.2024, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court has observed that:
"Whether the appellant can be granted the benefit of the new legislation and be awarded a lesser punishment as is presently prescribed under the new law. This court in T. Barai VS. Henry Ah Hoe (1983) 1 SCC 177, had held that when an amendment is beneficial to the accused it can be applied even to cases pending the courts where Ajay Kumar vs Food Inspector on 26 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/40683698/
5 such a provision did not exist at the time of commission of offence." 
19. The recent judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in case M/s A. K. Sarkar & Company &
Anr.(supra) has made it clear that if there is an amendment in the Act, which is beneficial to the accused, it can be applied even to the pending cases in the court where such provision was not in existence. The ratio of judgment M/s A. K. Sarkar & Company & Anr.(supra) is squarely applicable to the facts of present case. Therefore on the basis of above case law, I have no hesitation to hold that this court can take a lenient view as per new provisions of law. 
20. In the present case the complaint was filed on 28.06.2011. The appellant was held guilty and convicted for the offences punishable under Section 16(1)(a) of PFA Act for selling adulterated food in violation of Section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act and has been sentenced to simple imprisonment for one year as well as to pay fine of Rs.25,000/- and to undergo simple imprisonment for 15 days in default of payment of fine. The appellant has already faced the trauma of trial for almost 12 years. 
The appellant is not previously convict nor Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector involved in any other case. The circumstances disclosed by Ld.counsel for the appellant/convict also warrants taking of a lenient view. Considering all the aspects; nature of offence as alleged, submissions made, a lenient view is taken and the sentence imposed by the Ld. Trial court vide order dated 03.02.2017 for commission of offence under Section 16(1)(a) of PFA Act is modified and the appellant/convicted is sentenced to pay fine of Rs.50,000/-. The fine of Rs.25,000/- is already stated to have deposited before the Ld. Trial Court. The remaining fine amount shall be deposited by the appellant before the concerned court within a period of 15 days from today. In case of default of payment of fine, the appellant shall undergo simple imprisonment for a period of 30 days. Appeal is accordingly partly allowed. 
21. Attested copy of the judgment be given to the appellant/convict, free of cost. Trial court record be sent back to the court concerned alongwith copy of this order. 
22. Appeal file be consigned to record room after necessary compliance. 
Announced in the open court On this 26th of April, 2024 (Devender Kumar Jangala) Additional Sessions Judge-05 NDD/PHC/New Delhi.

summary.ANALYSIS:
The learned Trial Court has rightly come to observation that there is no rule prescribed under the statute to conclude what variation would be substantial enough to be considered in favour of the accused.
The Act or Rules do not prescribe that any variation of more than a specific value or percentage would be a substantial variation so as to disregard the report of the CFL which has otherwise been given finality or conclusiveness.
In the absence of any such standard Ajay Kumar Vs.
Food Inspector prescribed, the matter would be governed only by the evidence adduced by the parties, which includes cross-examination of witnesses(subject to cross-examination of course).
I am in agreement with the observation made by Ld. Trial Court that no benefit can be granted to the accused merely because there are variations in two reports.
If the accused is able to show through evidence that the variations are substantial enough so as to conclude that the sample was not representative, he would get benefit.
It is true that in the present case the accused has fails to show that such variations were due to sample being not representative.
There is no requirement under the Act or Rules that the two reports should be uniform or identical or that any variation of +- 0.3% in any ingredient would nullify the report of CFL.

The CFL report has confirmed the PA report on both the counts, though the percentage of light berries exceeded a little by the time the sample reached the CFL but as far as mineral oil is concerned, the CFL has confirmed the PA report.
During the course of trial no stand has been taken by the accused that any such oil was as a result of natural involvement or the food article having been exposed to the natural environment.
There is nothing on record to disbelieve the reports relied upon by the prosecution wherein the mineral oil has been detected in the food article.
The appellant is not previously convict nor Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector involved in any other case.
